summary:
Caldas stands under the national framework of Colombia, where legal gender recognition rests on self-recognition. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

No finding specific to Caldas on law, enforcement practice or incidents affecting trans people appears in the sources available for this record. The reporting these sources carry is national in scope or concerns other departments, and nothing in it marks Caldas as materially safer or more dangerous than Colombia as a whole.

The national baseline against which a visitor to Caldas is assessed is violent. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025, and one report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of that year. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

Targeted killings of trans people occur in ordinary urban settings as well as conflict-affected territory. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was beaten in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia in April 2025, filmed by onlookers and thrown into a creek, and died the following afternoon; the El País English edition reported on 14 April 2025 that no one had been arrested. Her death provoked national outrage and mobilisations against transphobia, and President Petro ordered an urgent investigation.
tangentialFactors:
The sharpest documented risk to trans people in Colombia sits where armed groups operate, and the documented campaigns are located outside Caldas. The Guardian's investigation of 30 July 2024 records armed groups in Caquetá giving trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed and circulating "social cleansing" flyers against trans women, with trans women in that department reporting few options beyond sex work. In Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". Neither report contains Caldas-specific information.

Accountability for these killings is contested. An activist quoted in The Guardian states that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording the killings as ordinary cases. The same investigation reports 41 trans women killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024, while the Attorney General's Office count for January to May 2025 stands at 35 LGBTI murders.

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.

Colombia's formal legal position is comparatively protective: marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and the UN Independent Expert's May 2025 mission praised the government's reforms even as he warned of the gap with lived experience.
localsOnly:
For residents of Caldas, changing the sex marker on government-issued identification requires only a document signed before a notary, a route open since June 2015. The official Reyes, who defended that change, described the examinations it replaced as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice".

Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition with no surgical requirement, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

The courts have also intervened directly in detention: a Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Caldas-specific source on law, enforcement practice, incidents, facilities, healthcare access or protection machinery was available for this record, so the department's position is carried by national reporting alone. Whether armed-group activity documented in Caquetá and Guajira extends into Caldas is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

The counts cited nationally (35 LGBTI murders from January to May 2025, 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025, 41 trans women killed in 2023, eight between February and April 2024) are not broken down by department in these sources, so whether any recorded killing occurred in Caldas is unresolved. The claim that prosecutors record transfemicide as ordinary cases rests on an activist's statement to The Guardian and is not independently verified in this record. Whether the notary procedure for marker changes is applied without obstacle in Caldas, and how the pending comprehensive trans law would affect residents, are likewise not sourced.
